title: Design patterns that still matter
subtitle: Learn the few design patterns you will meet every week, how modern languages made them smaller, and how to spot a pattern that makes code worse.

They needed one simple pattern. They got four, and one added hidden global state.

A design pattern is a named answer to a problem that keeps coming back in a certain situation. The idea comes from building design. Venners describes Alexander's architecture work as having "inspired the software patterns movement".
In 1977, Christopher Alexander and his co-authors published
. It has more than 250 patterns for towns and buildings. Each has a problem, a discussion and a solution.
In 1994, Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides published
. People call them the "Gang of Four" (GoF). The publisher describes it as "a catalog of simple and succinct solutions to commonly occurring design problems", with 23 patterns.
A pattern gives you two things. The first is a shared name. Gamma says patterns "provide you with a vocabulary to describe and discuss a particular design."
The second is a set of trade-offs, not "a pat solution" (a ready-made answer).

Many patterns have become smaller since 1994. In 1996, Peter Norvig found that "16 of 23 patterns are either invisible or simpler" in Lisp or Dylan. He compared them with C++, for at least some uses of each pattern.
He called a pattern invisible when it is "so much a part of language that you don't notice".

This ties each subclass to its parent. Gamma says inheritance is "brittle, because the subclass can easily make assumptions about the context".

Gamma warns: "Trying to use all the patterns is a bad thing, because you will end up with synthetic designs."
He advises: "Do not start immediately throwing patterns into a design". He likes to use them "after the fact, refactoring to patterns".

q.v: A function picks a shipping price with a switch over 12 carriers. New carriers arrive every month, and a change for one carrier once broke another. What is the simplest good fix in TypeScript?

options.v: A map from carrier name to a pricing function, with a clear error for unknown carriers.
An abstract base class, a factory and a singleton registry of carrier classes.
Keep the switch and add more comments.

why.v: The problem is one decision with many variants. With first-class functions, a Strategy can be just a function value.

q.v: Your tests pass alone but fail when run together in a different order. The code reads its config through Config.getInstance(). What is the likely cause?

options.v: A singleton keeps global state between tests, and the code hides that it depends on it.

why.v: Hevery calls singletons "nothing more than global state". Classes then use things their APIs do not declare.

q.v: You must add timing around many fee rules, without editing each rule. Which approach fits?

options.v: Builder. Give each rule a builder object.
Singleton. Put one global timer inside every rule.
Decorator. A function takes a rule and returns a timed rule with the same signature.

why.v: A decorator wraps a call and keeps the same interface, so callers and rules do not change.

q.v: What did Erich Gamma advise about when to apply patterns?

options.v: Use them as you go, once the problem shows up, by refactoring toward them.
Plan all patterns at the start, before you write code.
Use as many as you can, so the design is flexible.

why.v: Gamma prefers "refactoring to patterns" and warns that trying to use all of them gives "synthetic designs".
